body: Commercial safety is not only mechanical: before an airline captain can legally disengage the parking brake, they must hold a valid first-class medical certificate — a temporary operating permit, not a lifetime award, that can vanish overnight through routine aging, bureaucratic delay or an unexpected physiological hurdle. Under Federal Aviation Administration rules, any pilot exercising Airline Transport Pilot privileges must hold a valid first-class medical certificate, valid for 12 months for pilots under 40 and just six months for those 40 and older, requiring biannual evaluations by an Aviation Medical Examiner to catch age-related cardiovascular and systemic issues early. In the UK or Europe, the 12-month validity extends to age 60, though for pilots over 40 in single-pilot commercial operations the period matches the FAA's six months. An expired first-class certificate does not instantly ground a pilot completely: it automatically downgrades to second- and third-class privileges for designated periods, allowing the pilot to continue as a first officer or private pilot depending on time elapsed.

Beneath renewals sits the rigid framework of Part 67, which lists exactly 15 specific medical conditions that immediately bar anyone from holding any class of medical certificate. Cardiovascular disorders dominate aviation medicine: AOPA data indicates heart disease grounds more professional and private pilots than any other medical category combined, and a history of myocardial infarction, chronic angina, heart valve replacements, permanent cardiac pacemakers and full heart transplants are instant red flags halting a career until thoroughly reviewed. Neurological and psychological conditions — epilepsy, unexplained disturbances of consciousness, bipolar disorder, psychosis and severe personality disorders — are absolute statutory barriers, as are substance dependence without two consecutive years of documented, verified recovery and insulin-requiring diabetes. The shared logic is to weed out physiological vulnerabilities that could suddenly incapacitate a crew member.

A disqualifying diagnosis is not necessarily the end. The Federal Air Surgeon's discretionary Special Issuance lets aviators who can clinically prove they pose no undue risk to flight safety gain certification through rigorous case-by-case review, typically with strict expiration constraints, often 12-month renewals and ongoing physiological monitoring; several thousand pilots with successfully treated cardiovascular conditions continue flying commercial routes through this pathway. For substance abuse or psychological hurdles, the route back runs through the HIMS program, combining peer support, strict psychiatric monitoring and random chemical screenings. In July 2026 the FAA introduced AME-Assisted Special Issuance pathways, empowering certified Aviation Medical Examiners to handle renewals locally for pilots managing specific treated anxiety and depression conditions once an initial federal determination has established clinical stability — previously even minor adjustments to an approved medication regimen could ground capable pilots for months in bureaucratic backlog. In September 2026 the administration proposed overhauling diabetes disqualifications, acknowledging that continuous glucose monitoring provides real-time tracking, so pilots managing metabolic conditions with non-insulin medications would no longer face automatic bars — though this remains a pending proposal, not a finalized rule. Congress is moving too: the bipartisan John A. Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act, already passed by the Senate, proposes allocating up to $15 million annually through 2028 to recruit and train aviation medical examiners and streamline the Special Issuance backlog. And even with a pristine certificate, pilots carry a legal duty of self-grounding: they are barred from exercising privileges if they know or suspect any condition renders them temporarily unfit, because paper certification never supersedes actual wellness.
en.summary: A first-class medical certificate is the precondition for flying as an airline pilot: 12 months' validity under 40, six months at 40 and over; Part 67 lists 15 absolute disqualifying conditions, with heart disease the biggest grounding cause. Special Issuance and the HIMS program offer routes back, and 2026 reforms and pending legislation aim to cut the administrative burden.
en.title: How medical certificates can actually ground airline pilots

body: 商業飛行的安全不只取決於機械與航電：航空公司機長在鬆開停車煞車之前，必須持有有效的一級體檢證照。體檢證照不是終身成就，而是一張有期限的營運許可，可能因例行老化、行政延誤或突發健康問題一夜失效。根據美國聯邦航空總署規定，行使航線運輸駕駛員權限的機師必須持有有效的一級體檢證照；未滿40歲者效期12個月，40歲以上縮短為6個月，須每半年接受航空醫學檢查員評估，以便及早發現與年齡相關的心血管與全身性問題。在英國或歐洲，12個月效期適用至60歲；40歲以上執行單人駕駛商用飛行者，效期同樣縮為6個月，與美國規定一致。證照過期並不會讓機師立刻完全停飛：效期屆滿後，證照會自動降級為二級與三級權限一段特定期間，機師仍可擔任副駕駛或私人飛行員，視經過的時間而定。

真正的硬性界線在聯邦航空規章第67部：該部明列15項特定醫療狀況，罹患其中任何一項即無法持有任何等級的體檢證照。心血管疾病在航空醫學中佔據最重要位置；據AOPA彙整的資料，心臟疾病導致停飛的機師人數超過其他所有醫療類別的總和。心肌梗塞病史、慢性心絞痛、心臟瓣膜置換、永久性心臟節律器與心臟移植，都是立即叫停職涯發展的紅旗。神經與心理方面的絕對禁令包括癲癇、不明原因意識障礙、雙相情緒障礙、精神病與嚴重人格障礙；物質依賴須有連續2年經文件證實的康復紀錄，胰島素依賴型糖尿病同樣在列。這些規定的共同邏輯，是排除可能在飛行中突然失能的生理弱點。

遇到禁令並非職涯終點。聯邦航空醫官可依個案裁量核發「特別核發」許可：機師若能以臨床證據證明不構成不當飛安風險，即可經嚴格逐案審查取得證照；這類有條件許可通常附有嚴格效期限制，往往須每12個月更新並持續接受生理監測。據統計，數千名心血管疾病經成功治療的機師，正是透過這條管道繼續執飛商用航線。物質濫用或心理障礙者的復飛管道則是HIMS計畫：結合同儕支持、嚴格精神監測與隨機化驗，形成完整的復健與問責機制。2026年7月，聯邦航空總署正式引進「航空醫學檢查員協助特別核發」管道：對於已確立臨床穩定的特定焦慮與憂鬱症機師，檢查員可在地辦理續證，不必再將文件送往地區航醫辦公室；過去即使只是微調核准藥物劑量，也常因行政積壓讓有能力的機師停飛數月。2026年9月，當局進一步提出糖尿病禁令改革草案：承認連續血糖監測技術可即時追蹤生理狀態，對於以非胰島素藥物控制代謝狀況的機師，不再自動設限；但這仍是待決草案，而非已定規則。國會也在推動立法：已獲參議院通過的《約翰·A·豪瑟航空心理健康法案》擬每年撥款最高1,500萬美元至2028年，用於招募與培訓航空醫學檢查員、清理特別核發積案。即使持有完好無缺的證照，機師仍負有「自我停飛」的法定義務：若明知或懷疑自己有暫時不適飛的身心狀況，就不得行使權限——紙面證照永遠不能取代實際健康狀態。
zh.summary: 一級體檢證照是機師合法執飛的前提：未滿40歲效期12個月，40歲以上僅6個月；聯邦航空規章第67部明列15項絕對禁令，心血管疾病是最大停飛原因。特別核發與HIMS計畫提供復飛管道，2026年的新制與國會立法正試圖減輕行政負擔。
zh.title: 航空體檢證照如何讓機師停飛：效期、15項禁令與復飛管道解析
